Hi all,
Same problem here: my game randomly stops (audio still playing) after having upgraded my Mac Mini M1 Pro to macOS Tahoe.
Good luck to the fixers! :)

I did a fairly deep investigation of what appears to be the same Metal failure mode on Apple Silicon, and I have some additional evidence that may help narrow this issue down.

The main finding is:

> **In my reproduction, `timeout waiting for fence` is not the primary failure. It happens after a real Metal GPU page fault.**

I instrumented an exact Godot 4.7.1 build and was able to identify the faulting Metal compute pipeline consistently, then checked the CPU-visible buffer bounds, resource lifetime, argument-buffer composition, and Metal residency path.

At this point I have stopped local CPU-side debugging because all of those invariants are clean at the time of the fault.

## Environment

- **Godot:** 4.7.1-stable
- **Exact source base:** `a13da4feb8d8aefc283c3763d33a2f170a18d541`
- **Platform:** macOS 26.5.2 / Darwin 25.5.0
- **Architecture:** arm64
- **GPU:** Apple M1 Pro (Apple7)
- **Renderer:** Forward+
- **Backend:** Metal
- `GODOT_MTL_FORCE_BARRIERS` is **not set**
- Real city-simulation workload with many animated/skinned meshes

The project itself was kept unchanged throughout the engine-side investigation.

---

## 1. What actually happens before `timeout waiting for fence`

I added diagnostics for:

- `MTLCommandBufferErrorOptionEncoderExecutionStatus`
- Metal command-buffer completion errors
- semantic labels for render / compute / blit encoders
- encoder execution states
- fence expected/signaled values
- signaling command-buffer status

Across **8 captured GPU page faults**, the failing encoder has always been the same compute pipeline:

```text
SkeletonShaderRD:1
```

which corresponds to:

```text
SkeletonShader::SHADER_MODE_3D
```

issued from:

```text
MeshStorage::update_mesh_instances()
```

Example failure:

```text
[PD-METAL] COMMAND BUFFER FAILED:
label="Godot Frame Command Buffer #5855"
status=Error
error="Caused GPU Address Fault Error
(0000000b:kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorPageFault)"

[PD-METAL] encoder[7] state=Faulted
label="[7] compute | Command Graph (L1) (Copy+Compute) |
pipeline=\"SkeletonShaderRD:1\""

[PD-METAL] encoder[8] state=Pending
label="[8] compute | ... |
pipeline=\"VolumetricFogShaderRD:2\""
```

The surrounding render encoders can complete normally while the skeleton compute encoder faults.

The failure sequence I observe is:

```text
SkeletonShaderRD GPU page fault
        ↓
additional GPU faults
        ↓
kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorSubmissionsIgnored
        ↓
MTLSharedEvent stops progressing
        ↓
Godot starts reporting:
"timeout waiting for fence"
```

So, at least in this workload, the fence timeout is a **downstream symptom** of an earlier GPU address fault.

---

## 2. Fence retry does not recover this case

I also tested the caller-side fence retry approach discussed earlier in this issue.

The idea was to retry `fence_wait()` in the caller and not reset/reuse the associated command pool/frame resources until the fence actually signals.

Result:

```text
139 retries
0 recoveries
```

Once Metal had started returning:

```text
kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorSubmissionsIgnored
```

the expected shared-event value never arrived.

So I think retrying is safer than pretending a failed wait succeeded, but in this particular failure mode it cannot recover the process because the fence timeout occurs **after** the GPU has already faulted / entered the submissions-ignored state.

---

## 3. The faulting pass is 3D GPU skinning

All captured page faults so far:

```text
8 / 8
```

have identified:

```text
pipeline="SkeletonShaderRD:1"
```

The workload contains both:

- rigged character meshes with 31- and 62-bone skeletons
- wind-animated foliage using 3-bone skeletons

Some of the foliage also has active blend shapes and goes through the same `SkeletonShaderRD` path.

A typical faulting compute encoder contains roughly:

```text
336–362 SkeletonShader dispatches
```

and the workload reaches roughly:

```text
~200–300 skinning dispatches per frame
```

depending on simulation state.

A synthetic project with skinned meshes did **not** reproduce the problem, so this is not evidence that GPU skinning in general is broken.

The real workload shape appears to matter.

---

## 4. I validated the actual SkeletonShader buffer addressing

Because the failing pipeline was so consistent, I instrumented the exact addressing used by `skeleton.glsl`.

For every dispatch I checked CPU-side:

- destination vertex-buffer allocation size
- maximum destination write offset
- source vertex-buffer allocation and maximum read offset
- skin-buffer allocation / stride / weight offsets
- active blend-shape buffers and weights
- skeleton bone-transform buffer size
- maximum referenced joint index
- skeleton bone count
- mesh/surface generations
- mesh-instance output-buffer generation
- relevant uniform-set/resource generations

Across three new page-fault reproductions:

```text
1536 SkeletonShader dispatch records checked
0 bounds violations
```

### Destination buffer

For every recorded dispatch:

```text
allocated_bytes >= maximum_shader_write_bytes
```

In many cases the buffer is exactly tightly sized to the maximum valid address.

There were no negative margins and no stale surface-generation mismatch.

### Source vertex / skin buffers

All source vertex and skin-buffer reads were in range.

Typical skin configuration was:

```text
skin_stride=4
skin_weight_offset=2
```

and the required range always matched the actual allocation.

### Bone transforms / joint indices

For every recorded surface:

```text
max_joint_index < bone_count
```

Examples included:

- 3-bone foliage skeletons
- 31-bone character skeletons
- 62-bone character skeletons

No out-of-range joint index was found.

### Blend shapes

An earlier summary of mine incorrectly stated that blend shapes were inactive in all recorded dispatches.

That was wrong.

Out of the 1536 recorded dispatches:

```text
348
```

had:

```text
has_blend_shape=1
blend_shape_count=2
```

These were wind-tree surfaces.

Their blend-shape buffers and blend-weight buffers were also correctly sized:

```text
allocated == required
```

with no bounds violations.

The correction does not change the CPU-bounds result.

---

## 5. The faults also occur in steady state

This does not appear to require a mesh or skeleton to have just been created or destroyed.

For two of the reproduced faults, there had been:

```text
0 relevant output-buffer creations within 300 frames
0 relevant skeleton-buffer creations within 300 frames
```

before the fault.

So a simple immediate create/free lifetime race in `MeshStorage::update_mesh_instances()` does not currently fit the evidence.

---

## 6. I then checked the Metal residency path

The next theory was that one of the GPU buffers might be correctly addressed but not resident when Metal dereferences it.

A useful discovery here is that the `MTLResidencySet` path is **not active at all** in my configuration.

In 4.7.1:

```cpp
bool barriers_enabled =
        OS::get_singleton()->get_environment(
                "GODOT_MTL_FORCE_BARRIERS") == "1";
```

With that unset:

```text
use_barriers=false
main_residency_set=absent
```

So `_track_resource()` / `_untrack_resource()` do not actually populate the residency add/remove vectors in this configuration.

There is no `MTLResidencySet` participating in the fault.

Instead, resources referenced through argument buffers are made resident with per-encoder:

```text
useResources()
```

So I instrumented that real path instead.

---

## 7. Per-encoder `useResources()` residency is also clean

The residency instrumentation covered:

```text
14,182 Metal encoders
1,688,715 resource residency grants
```

Result:

```text
0 cross-encoder residency skips
```

All relevant resource-tracking calls also came from a single thread.

For every encoder, including the encoder that actually produced the GPU page fault, every resource referenced through the SkeletonShader argument buffers was made resident with `useResources()` on that exact encoder.

The checked resource types include:

- destination vertex buffer
- source vertex buffer
- skin buffer
- active blend-shape buffer
- active blend-weight buffer
- skeleton / bone-transform buffer

I found no case where a SkeletonShader dispatch referenced a real resource that had not been made resident on its encoder.

---

## 8. Argument-buffer resource tracking also appears complete

I audited the uniform-set / argument-buffer path.

The flow is effectively:

```text
uniform_set_create
    ↓
ADD_USAGE for bound nested resources
    ↓
usage_to_resources
    ↓
merge_from()
    ↓
ResourceTracker::encode()
    ↓
useResources()
```

Every uniform type participates in `ADD_USAGE`; the default case asserts.

I found no nested argument-buffer resource that bypassed the tracker.

The argument buffers themselves are directly bound with Metal `setBuffer`, so they do not depend on the nested-resource residency mechanism.

---

## 9. The argument-buffer copy queue also appears correctly ordered

Another possible concern was the copy queue used to populate argument-buffer contents.

It uses an unretained-reference command buffer, which initially looked suspicious.

However, the ordering is:

```text
copy queue encode
    ↓
commit()
    ↓
waitUntilCompleted()
    ↓
only afterwards submit the command buffer that consumes the argument buffer
```

So the GPU copy of the argument-buffer contents is complete before the consuming command buffer can execute.

I also checked the dynamic argument-buffer scratch allocator.

It is reset per command buffer and grows rather than wrapping over allocations still needed by an unexecuted encoder.

I could not reproduce a stale/overwritten argument-buffer address from those paths.

---

## 10. Resource lifetime / free ordering also looks valid

In this configuration `_untrack_resource()` is a no-op because explicit residency sets are disabled.

The Metal resource release itself happens in the driver only after `RenderingDevice` has deferred the resource into the frame disposal list and waited for the relevant frame fence.

I found no CPU-visible case where a buffer was freed while an in-flight command buffer still needed it.

Again, this does **not** prove Metal's internal state is correct — only that the CPU-side lifetime contract visible in Godot appears correct.

---

## 11. Current strongest conclusion

At the time `SkeletonShaderRD:1` page-faults, the CPU can verify that its resources are:

- correctly sized
- addressed within their valid ranges
- using valid skin/joint indices
- backed by valid-looking Godot resources
- correctly composed into the argument buffers
- not prematurely freed according to RenderingDevice's lifetime
- explicitly passed to `useResources()` on the encoder that uses them

and Metal still reports:

```text
kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorPageFault
```

So I no longer have evidence for a safe CPU-side Godot fix.

The remaining ambiguity is below what encoder-level CPU instrumentation can observe.

One `SkeletonShaderRD` compute encoder contains hundreds of individual compute dispatches, while:

```text
MTLCommandBufferEncoderInfo
```

only tells me that the encoder faulted.

It does not tell me which individual dispatch/thread/address inside that encoder caused the GPU page fault.

---

## 12. A separate `ResourceTracker` observation

During the residency audit I noticed one unrelated potential issue worth mentioning.

`ResourceTracker::_previous` appears to memoize resource usage for the duration of an encoder, but it is reset at the encoding-session level.

A new compute encoder can be created on a pipeline change without necessarily resetting that memo.

Conceptually this could lead to:

```text
resource was made resident on encoder A
        ↓
new encoder B
        ↓
memo says resource usage already satisfied
        ↓
useResources() accidentally skipped for encoder B
```

which would be incorrect because `useResources()` residency is per encoder.

However, I instrumented exactly this condition during the failing workload and got:

```text
cross_encoder_skips=0
```

across the 1.69 million residency grants.

So I do **not** believe this caused my page fault.

I mention it only as a separate code-path observation that may be worth reviewing.

---

## 13. Interesting behavior after an isolated page fault

In the most recent run I got one `SkeletonShaderRD:1` GPU page fault at roughly:

```text
~75 seconds
```

but after that the application continued for approximately:

```text
28,000 additional frames
~14 minutes
```

without:

```text
SubmissionsIgnored
```

and without entering the fence-timeout storm.

Earlier instrumentation versions printed several thousand lines on every failure and tended to accumulate additional faults / reach the submissions-ignored state sooner.

The latest diagnostics reduced failure logging substantially.

I am **not claiming logging caused the problem**, but this run suggests that a single page fault does not necessarily immediately quarantine the Metal process.

The unrecoverable fence storm seems to occur after GPU faults accumulate and macOS begins rejecting later command buffers.

---

## 14. What I think is needed next

At this point I believe CPU-side diagnostics for my reproduction are exhausted.

The missing information is GPU-side:

> **Which individual `SkeletonShaderRD` dispatch/thread performs the access that causes the page fault, and which resource/address is involved?**

The next useful step seems to be a full Xcode Metal GPU capture / Shader Validation run on the real reproducing workload.

In particular, I would like to test with Metal Shader Validation enabled, potentially including:

```text
MTL_SHADER_VALIDATION=1
MTL_SHADER_VALIDATION_GLOBAL_MEMORY=1
MTL_SHADER_VALIDATION_TEXTURE_USAGE=1
```

and possibly:

```text
MTL_DEBUG_LAYER=1
```

if those are appropriate for this case.

I do not currently have the full Xcode Metal developer tools installed on this machine, so I stopped here instead of continuing to guess at CPU-side fixes.

The difficult part is also that time-to-failure varies from roughly one to several minutes, so a manually timed capture may be inconvenient.

A capture triggered around the failing command-buffer completion may be more practical if Metal allows that workflow.

---

## Summary

My current failure chain is:

```text
heavy SkeletonShaderRD workload
        ↓
MTL GPU address/page fault
        ↓
additional GPU faults may accumulate
        ↓
macOS starts returning SubmissionsIgnored
        ↓
MTLSharedEvent no longer reaches expected value
        ↓
Godot reports timeout waiting for fence
```

And so far I have ruled out, on the CPU-visible side:

- SkeletonShader destination-buffer overruns
- source vertex-buffer overruns
- skin-buffer overruns
- blend-shape-buffer overruns
- invalid joint indices
- undersized bone-transform buffers
- stale mesh-surface generations
- obvious skeleton uniform-set mismatch
- argument-buffer copy ordering
- missing nested argument-buffer resource tracking
- per-encoder `useResources()` residency omissions
- multi-threaded residency-vector races in this configuration
- obvious premature buffer disposal

I therefore think the visible `timeout waiting for fence` can, at least in some cases, be the **aftermath of an earlier Metal GPU page fault**, rather than the root failure itself.

If this is useful to the maintainers, I can provide the diagnostic patches I used for:

- Metal command-buffer / encoder labeling
- encoder execution-state reporting
- SkeletonShader CPU bounds validation
- per-encoder argument-buffer residency validation

and I would be happy to run a specific additional experiment or Metal capture configuration if there is something in particular you would like checked.

Hey @stuartcarnie,

Thanks — I ran both tests you suggested on the same saved-game reproduction and automated workload.

### 1. `GODOT_MTL_DISABLE_ARGUMENT_BUFFERS=1`

Argument buffers are **not required** for the fault.

I verified that the variable affects Metal shader compilation in Godot 4.7.1, so before the OFF test I cleared the shared project shader cache and performed a dedicated cold warm-up with the variable already enabled.

I also verified the rebuilt cache contents changed from:

```text
MetalDeviceProfile::Features::use_argument_buffers: 1 -> 0
HeaderData::flags: USES_ARGUMENT_BUFFERS -> NONE
```

Results:

| Backend | Duration | Page faults | Faulting pipeline | `SubmissionsIgnored` | Fence timeouts |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| Metal, argument buffers **ON** | 30 min | 3, first at 73 s | `SkeletonShaderRD:1` | 5394 | 1676 |
| Metal, argument buffers **OFF** | 30 min warm | 2, first at 829 s | `SkeletonShaderRD:1` | 3469 | 942 |

The argument-buffer-OFF warm-up run also faulted, at about 146 s after gameplay started.

The failure signature remained the same at the encoder level:

```text
kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorPageFault
pipeline="SkeletonShaderRD:1"
```

followed later by:

```text
kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorSubmissionsIgnored
```

and then the fence timeout cascade.

So this looks like **CASE AB-2: argument buffers are not required for the fault**.

The large difference in first-fault latency (73 s vs 829 s) is only one stochastic sample, so I would not infer that disabling argument buffers makes the workload safer.

One potentially useful side observation: clearing the shader cache really is necessary for this test. In 4.7.1, the argument-buffer state does not appear to be part of the shader-cache key, so a previously cached argument-buffer shader can otherwise be reloaded even when `GODOT_MTL_DISABLE_ARGUMENT_BUFFERS=1` is set.

### 2. Vulkan / MoltenVK

I then ran the identical save, automated workload, 1600x900 window and Forward+ renderer using:

```text
--rendering-driver vulkan
```

Startup reported:

```text
Vulkan 1.2.334 - Forward+ - Apple M1 Pro
```

Results:

```text
30 minutes
0 crashes
0 device lost
0 GPU errors
0 SCRIPT ERROR
no stalls
26–45 fps
```

The simulation remained fully interactive and visually correct through the entire run.

For comparison:

- native Metal with argument buffers ON faulted first at 73 s
- native Metal with argument buffers OFF faulted first at 829 s
- Vulkan/MoltenVK stayed clean for the full 30-minute run

So at the moment this **strongly points toward the native Metal path**, rather than argument buffers specifically or renderer-independent `MeshStorage` logic.

I would still treat this as strong evidence rather than absolute proof because the fault is stochastic. The longest clean Metal stretch I have previously observed was about 14 minutes.

### MRP

I still don't have a reduced MRP.

The smaller synthetic cases I've tried remain clean, including:

- ~80 procedurally skinned meshes
- thousands of spawn/free cycles
- a heavier variant with clustered lighting, volumetric fog, SSAO, SSIL and shadows

The real workload that reproduces has approximately:

- 23 skinned citizens
- skinned / blend-shaped wind trees
- ~200–300 skinning dispatches per frame
- all skinning dispatches batched into one `SkeletonShaderRD:1` compute encoder
- TAA / motion vectors
- MSAA 4x at 1920x1080
- volumetric fog
- large shadow-atlas passes
- continuous camera / weather / view-mode / 1x–4x workload churn

# metalgpufault

Procedural Godot project, no assets. On screen: a field of waving green blades, orbiting camera. Every object is the same bone-chained tapered tube — only counts and update cadence matter.

- 25 heavy meshes: 1176 verts, 31/62-bone chains, skinned every frame (stand-ins for NPCs).
- 900 light meshes: 72 verts, 3-bone chains, 2 blend shapes, skinned every 1–6 frames, reshuffled each second (stand-ins for foliage).
- TAA, MSAA 4x, volumetric fog, 4 shadow-casting lights, 10 meshes freed/respawned every 2 s.
- Net: 252 skinning dispatches in one compute encoder per frame.

Three things were needed to make it fault: staggered cadence (Godot only double-buffers a mesh skinned within the last 2 frames, so always-animating meshes never re-enter that path), meshes on screen (offscreen meshes aren't skinned), and a large enough batch (tuned against a GPU capture to 252 dispatches).

## Repro

Defaults are the faulting config — no env vars, no arguments.

```sh
./Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --path metalgpufault --rendering-driver metal -- --minutes=2
```

Debug build, M1 Max / macOS 26.5.1, window visible. Faults in 1–2 min. M4 Max never faults. `GODOT_MTL_DISABLE_ARGUMENT_BUFFERS=1` makes it far worse: 401 failures and a hang in 10 min.

```
Metal command buffer failed: Caused GPU Address Fault Error
  encoder[3] faulted: 3: SkeletonShaderRD:1
  encoder[4] pending: 4: ClusterStoreShaderRD:0
```

Then `timeout waiting for fence` every frame until it freezes.

Debug-only instrumentation in `drivers/metal/metal3_objects.cpp`: command buffers created with `CommandBufferErrorOptionEncoderExecutionStatus` plus a completion handler dumping encoder states, and compute encoders named after their first pipeline. Without it you only see the fence timeout, which points at the wrong place.

## Current interpretation

So I get the same result in both the minimal repro and the real workload:

```text
hazard tracking + DispatchTypeConcurrent
    -> reproduces

barriers + DispatchTypeConcurrent
    -> no reproduction in tested window

hazard tracking + DispatchTypeSerial
    -> no reproduction in tested window
```

That seems like strong evidence that the failure is related to the native Metal concurrent/hazard-synchronization path rather than invalid skeleton data itself.

However, I don't think these results are sufficient to distinguish the exact mechanism yet.

In the current #121392 revision, `barriers` changes more than just the placement of a single synchronization primitive: it also changes the synchronization model, disables Metal's automatic hazard tracking for the relevant resources, and uses the placement-heap path.

Likewise, `DispatchTypeSerial` may simply remove the overlap that exposes a missing dependency rather than fixing that dependency.

So I would not claim either experiment identifies the root cause by itself.

## Previous CPU-side checks

For context, the earlier diagnostics on the real workload still stand:

```text
1,536 SkeletonShaderRD dispatches checked
0 CPU-visible buffer/addressing violations
```

including destination, source, skin, blend-shape, blend-weight and bone-transform buffers, plus joint-index validation.

And:

```text
14,182 Metal encoders
1,688,715 useResources() grants
0 cross-encoder residency gaps
```

So we still have no evidence that malformed buffer ranges or missing per-encoder resource residency are what triggers this.

## Caveats

The main caveat is that absence of failure is not proof.

The control latency is stochastic:

```text
MRP: ~20–78 seconds in these runs
real project: historically ~1–10 minutes
```

but 20 minutes on the MRP and ~32 minutes on the real workload are substantially beyond the observed control failure windows.
